questions.stem: Which function is analytic everywhere in the complex plane?
questions.solution: The function f(z) = z^2 is analytic everywhere because its derivative exists and is continuous for all z. A has a non-differentiable point at z=0, C has a singularity at z=0, and D has singularities at z=0 and integer multiples of πi.
questions.explanation: Analytic functions have continuous derivatives in their domain, allowing differentiation infinitely many times without issues like discontinuities or singularities.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students may choose A due to the smooth appearance of the absolute value function, but it's non-differentiable at z=0.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic in the region Re(z) > 0?
questions.solution: f(z) = cosh(z) is analytic in Re(z) > 0 as its derivative exists and is continuous for all z with positive real part. A is entire, B has a branch cut along the negative real axis, and D has singularities at ±∞.
questions.explanation: Analyticity depends on the function's derivative being continuous within its domain; here, we look for a function analytic in Re(z) > 0.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students might choose B, forgetting that ln(z) has a branch cut along the negative real axis.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic in the region |z| < 1?
questions.solution: f(z) = 1/(1-z) is analytic in |z| < 1 due to being a geometric series with radius of convergence 1. B is entire, C has a singularity at z=∞, and D has singularities at z=-1.
questions.explanation: Consider singularities and series convergence when assessing analyticity within a region.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students may choose B, thinking all polynomials are entire, but this one isn't restricted to the given region.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic in the upper half-plane Im(z) > 0?
questions.solution: f(z) = sinh(iz) is analytic in Im(z) > 0 as its derivative exists and is continuous for all z with positive imaginary part. A is entire, B has a branch cut along the real axis, and D is even and thus not analytic.
questions.explanation: Analyticity depends on the function's derivative being continuous; here, we look for a function analytic in Im(z) > 0.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students might choose D, forgetting that cosh(z) is even and not analytic everywhere.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic at z=1?
questions.solution: f(z) = e^(1/(z-1)) is analytic at z=1 because the singularity is removable. A has a simple pole, B has a removable singularity, and C has a logarithmic singularity.
questions.explanation: Analyticity requires differentiability except possibly at isolated singularities; here, we look for a function analytic at z=1.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students may choose B, thinking removing the singularity makes it analytic, but it's not defined at z=1.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic at z=i?
questions.solution: f(z) = e^(1/(z-i)) is analytic at z=i due to a removable singularity. A has a simple pole, B has a removable singularity, and C has a logarithmic singularity.
questions.explanation: Analyticity requires differentiability except possibly at isolated singularities; here, we look for a function analytic at z=i.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students may choose B, thinking removing the singularity makes it analytic, but it's not defined at z=i.

questions.stem: Which function is analytic in the region Re(z) < 0 and Im(z) ≠ 0?
questions.solution: f(z) = ln(z) is analytic in Re(z) < 0 and Im(z) ≠ 0 as its derivative exists and is continuous for z with negative real part and non-zero imaginary part. A is entire, C has a singularity at z=0, and D is even and not analytic.
questions.explanation: Check singularities and continuity of the derivative when assessing analyticity in a region.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Students might choose A, thinking all polynomials are entire, but this one isn't restricted to the given region.
